note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

constraints: ids match [A-Za-z0-9_]{1,20} and are unique across rows
clarifyingQuestions: Which payment types are refunded first, and in what order?
Within a type, is the most recent payment refunded first?
What happens when the refundable total is smaller than refundAmount?
Should payments that receive nothing be listed?
hints: A payment can only give back what has not already been refunded from it.
Sum the existing refunds per linked payment id once, in a hash map.
Sort the payments by (type rank, larger timestamp first, id) and hand out the amount greedily until it is used up.
invariants: each allocation is at most the payment's refundable balance
the allocations sum to min(refundAmount, total refundable)
chooseWhen: A fixed priority order decides who is refunded first
tradeoffs: Sorting all payments costs O(p log p) even when the first payment already covers the refund; a heap would stop earlier but is more code
hack2hire:68b996c98c4a0a9996afdd81.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: greedy refund allocation by type priority and recency

clarifyingQuestions: Should the answer be the list of valid lengths, their count, or the smallest one?
Is the whole string (one block) always counted?
hints: Only divisors of len(s) can be valid.
Prefix counts per letter give the letter counts of any block in O(26).
For each divisor L compare the counts of every block against the first block; stop at the first mismatch.
invariants: len(s) is always valid
a valid L divides len(s)
chooseWhen: Long strings with many divisors
tradeoffs: 26 prefix-count arrays use O(26n) memory; a rolling count per divisor uses O(26) memory but O(n) time per divisor anyway
hack2hire:6a330e686849fecc81440a3c.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: all valid prefix lengths

clarifyingQuestions: Is alphabetical order case-sensitive?
Is the word position 0-based, and does only the first matching word count?
Are duplicate names listed once or every time?
hints: Lower-case the prefix once and each word as you scan it.
For each name only the first matching word position matters.
Keep only the k smallest (position, name) keys; a bounded heap or a partial sort avoids sorting every match.
invariants: every returned name has a word starting with prefix (ignoring case)
returned keys are non-decreasing
chooseWhen: k is much smaller than the number of matches
tradeoffs: A bounded heap is O(m log k) but more code than one full sort, which is fine when k is close to m
hack2hire:67f5703f83ba2e5f057e6dfb.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: top k prefix matches by word position, then name

clarifyingQuestions: Are queries every prefix of one typed word, or an independent list?
Is the result capped (like the top 3 of LeetCode 1268)?
Is the alphabetical tie rule case-sensitive?
hints: Each query is the previous one plus one character, so the matching set only shrinks along the trie path.
Insert every lower-cased word into a trie, remembering which name and word position reached each node.
At each node on the searchWord path take the smallest word position per name and sort by (position, name).
invariants: a name matching searchWord[0:i+1] also matches searchWord[0:i]
within each list keys are non-decreasing
chooseWhen: Many names, a short typed word, all matches needed
tradeoffs: Storing (name, position) lists at every trie node costs memory proportional to total characters
hack2hire:67f8222b1d70a71460925c53.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: all matches for every typed prefix

clarifyingQuestions: Does an item expire when currentTime equals expiryTime?
When the cache is full, are all expired items removed or only one?
Does set on an existing key count as an access, and can it evict?
What does get return for a miss?
hints: Eviction needs the minimum of two different orders, so keep two heaps.
Recency only breaks ties: an increasing access stamp gives a total order.
Push a fresh heap entry on every access or update and skip entries whose stamp no longer matches the live item.
invariants: size never exceeds capacity
every live item has exactly one current entry in each heap
chooseWhen: Many operations with frequent evictions
tradeoffs: Lazy heaps can hold O(operations) stale entries; an indexed heap avoids that at the cost of more code
hack2hire:699f70796e73e4abccc9b539.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: cache with expiry, priority and LRU eviction

clarifyingQuestions: What exactly should be returned: sizes per second, the empty time, or the processing order?
Is the front process removed before or together with the expired ones?
Is time 0 included in the output?
hints: The simulation lasts at most n seconds because each second removes at least the front.
A process still present at time t has not been processed and has wait > t, so only waits up to n matter.
Count waits in buckets and move a front pointer past processes that are already gone.
invariants: sizes strictly decrease each second
the last size is 0
chooseWhen: Long queues where a literal re-filter each second would be quadratic
tradeoffs: Buckets need O(n) extra memory; sorting the waits instead would cost O(n log n)
hack2hire:67a2d68216a8465483dca727.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: queue size after every second

constraints: ids are unique and match [A-Za-z0-9_]{1,10}; neighborhoods match [A-Za-z0-9_]{1,10}
clarifyingQuestions: In what order are the selection rules applied?
Is a booked property unavailable forever?
What is returned when the group cannot be housed?
How are ties between equally good sets broken?
hints: The smallest possible number of properties is found by adding the largest capacities first.
Only sets of exactly that size can win, so enumerate just those combinations.
Enumerating combinations in id order means the first set with the smallest total is also the lexicographically smallest.
invariants: booked properties are never offered again
the returned set has total capacity >= groupSize
chooseWhen: Few properties per neighborhood, exact optimal choice needed
tradeoffs: Exponential in the neighborhood size; a capacity-indexed DP would scale further but makes the id tie rule harder
hack2hire:68b975348c4a0a9996afdd79.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: fewest, then tightest, then smallest-id group booking

clarifyingQuestions: How is randomness made testable: a seed, a supplied generator, or a list of draws?
Is the unmatched user reported, and how?
Must every pairing be equally likely, and how would you argue it?
hints: Drawing two distinct users uniformly at a time is a partial Fisher-Yates shuffle.
Removing a chosen user by moving the last one into its slot keeps the pool contiguous in O(1).
Use the draws strictly in order: first user, then second user of each pair.
invariants: each user appears in exactly one entry
the pool shrinks by exactly two per pair
chooseWhen: Large user lists where removing from the middle of a list would be quadratic
tradeoffs: Swap-with-last changes pool order, which is fine for uniformity but makes the result depend on the exact removal rule

clarifyingQuestions: Must paired users come from different groups?
Which groups are paired first when several have the same size?
Are unpaired users reported?
hints: Always pairing from the two largest groups maximises the number of pairs.
Keep each group's members in a queue in input order.
A max-heap of (count, name) gives the two largest groups; push a group back only while it still has members.
invariants: the two users of a pair are in different groups
at most one group has unpaired users at the end
chooseWhen: Many groups of uneven size
tradeoffs: The heap costs O(log g) per pair; with few groups a linear scan is as fast

constraints: next is only called when a value remains
clarifyingQuestions: What should next return, or throw, when the range is exhausted?
Is step 0 allowed?
Is end ever included?
hints: Store only the current value, not the whole range.
The direction of the comparison with end depends on the sign of step.
An empty range (start already at or past end) has no values at all.
invariants: current = start + (number of next calls) * step
hasNext never changes without a next call
chooseWhen: Huge ranges that must not be materialised
tradeoffs: None worth noting beyond handling the step sign

clarifyingQuestions: What is the result: reachability, the move count, or a number of paths?
Does a teleport count as a move?
Can teleports form loops, and what then?
Can an exit itself be an entrance?
hints: Because the robot only moves right, its path is completely determined; there is nothing to search.
Index teleports by entrance cell in a hash map.
Mark visited positions so a teleport cycle is detected instead of looping forever.
invariants: each position is occupied at most once on a successful walk
the move count never exceeds n*m
chooseWhen: Large grids with many teleports
tradeoffs: A visited array costs O(n*m) memory; counting steps against n*m would avoid it
hack2hire:69a3a0426e73e4abccc9c0e9.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: move count along the forced right-moving path

clarifyingQuestions: Is the window [t - W + 1, t] or (t - W, t]?
Do flagged requests count toward later windows?
Can timestamps arrive out of order?
hints: Only requests from the same IP inside the window matter.
Because timestamps never decrease, old requests can be dropped from the front of a per-IP queue for good.
After dropping, the queue length is the window count including the current request.
invariants: each per-IP queue holds exactly the requests inside the current window
every request is pushed once and popped at most once
chooseWhen: A real-time stream with many requests per IP
tradeoffs: Queues keep every in-window timestamp; a per-second bucket count would bound memory by the window size instead
hack2hire:68ad7692cdaebe9459ce9a78.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: sliding-window request counter per IP

clarifyingQuestions: Is the supply consumed by earlier recipes, or is each recipe checked alone?
Which characters can appear?
hints: Count the supply once.
For each recipe count its needs per character.
A recipe fails as soon as one character needs more than the supply holds.
invariants: the supply counts never change
the answer is at most recipes.length
chooseWhen: Many short recipes against one supply
tradeoffs: Fixed 26-entry arrays assume lowercase letters; a hash map handles any alphabet
hack2hire:67a43f105141b0ac3b8be4df.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: count independently preparable recipes

constraints: transaction ids are unique and match [A-Za-z0-9_]{1,20}; user ids match [A-Za-z0-9_]{1,20}
clarifyingQuestions: What does billing status mean: a balance, a label, or more?
Is a positive balance money owed by the user?
How are users ordered in the result?
hints: Treat an empty amount field as 0.
Each row changes one user's balance by charge minus payment.
Accumulate in a hash map and sort the user ids at the end.
invariants: row order does not change the final balance
every user with a row is reported
chooseWhen: Large unordered logs
tradeoffs: Sorting users costs O(u log u); the result order is fixed by the inferred spec
hack2hire:69499ed489ec36a1b1e2c13f.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: final balance per user

constraints: transaction ids are unique and match [A-Za-z0-9_]{1,20}; user ids match [A-Za-z0-9_]{1,20}
clarifyingQuestions: What does billing status mean: a balance, a label, or more?
Is a positive balance money owed by the user?
How are users ordered in the result?
Is a row at exactly the query timestamp included?
hints: Rows are unordered, so filter by timestamp instead of stopping early.
A user with rows only after the timestamp is not reported.
Accumulate charge minus payment per user and sort the ids.
invariants: only rows with timestamp <= the query count
increasing the query timestamp never removes a user
chooseWhen: One-off historical queries over an unordered log
tradeoffs: Many queries over the same log would favour sorting once and keeping prefix sums
hack2hire:6949a92289ec36a1b1e2c15c.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: balances as of a timestamp

constraints: transaction ids are unique and match [A-Za-z0-9_]{1,20}; user ids match [A-Za-z0-9_]{1,20}
clarifyingQuestions: What does billing status mean: a balance, a label, or more?
Is a positive balance money owed by the user?
How are users ordered in the result?
Which order is used for rows with the same timestamp?
Does the peak start at 0?
hints: The peak depends on order, so the rows must be replayed chronologically.
Sort all rows once by (timestamp, transactionId) instead of sorting per user.
Keep a running balance and a running maximum (starting at 0) per user.
invariants: peakBalance >= max(0, finalBalance)
finalBalance does not depend on row order
chooseWhen: Audit of outstanding exposure over time
tradeoffs: One global sort is O(t log t); bucketing by user first would sort smaller lists but needs more bookkeeping
hack2hire:6949b64a89ec36a1b1e2c16d.variantLabel: Inferred level 3: final and peak balance per user

constraints: op is plus, next or jump; value matches [+-]?(0|[1-9][0-9]{0,5}) with |value| <= 1e6
clarifyingQuestions: Should the result be the index, the accumulator, or both?
What if the program leaves the instruction range instead of repeating?
Is a "+" sign allowed on values?
hints: Each instruction has exactly one successor, so the run is a path that either leaves the range or enters a cycle.
Mark executed indices; the first index found marked is the repeat point.
Report the accumulator before executing the repeated instruction.
invariants: each instruction executes at most once before the stop
the accumulator only changes on plus
chooseWhen: Long programs
tradeoffs: A visited array costs O(n) memory; Floyd cycle detection would avoid it but returns a different index
hack2hire:6a373b356849fecc81442862.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: first repeated instruction and accumulator

constraints: the unmodified program does not reach index len
clarifyingQuestions: Which instructions may be switched?
If several switches work, which is reported?
Does leaving the range at any index other than len count as terminating?
hints: Only instructions on the original execution path matter: switching any other one leaves the run unchanged.
Compute, on the unmodified program, which indices reach len (walk the reverse edges from len).
A switch at i works exactly when its new successor reaches len; pick the smallest such i and replay to get the accumulator.
invariants: a working switch is on the original path
the repaired run executes each instruction at most once
chooseWhen: Long programs where trying every switch would be quadratic
tradeoffs: The reverse-edge pass needs an adjacency list of O(n) size

clarifyingQuestions: Should all valid strings, their count or one of them be returned?
If one, which one?
What is returned when none exists?
hints: The ? positions must supply exactly targetSum minus the fixed digits.
k remaining ? can supply any total from 0 to k * maxVal.
Going left to right, give each ? the smallest digit that keeps the remaining total reachable.
invariants: the remaining requirement stays within [0, remaining ? count * maxVal]
fixed digits are never changed
chooseWhen: Long patterns where backtracking would be exponential
tradeoffs: The greedy answer is one string; listing all solutions would need real backtracking
hack2hire:69ff8062574d87bc49006e92.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: lexicographically smallest restoration

clarifyingQuestions: What does setColor do before anything is selected?
Does setColor clear the selection?
Are indices 0-based?
hints: Painting a whole table or row cell by cell is too slow for large tables.
Remember each paint at the level it was applied (table, row or cell) with an increasing stamp.
A cell's color is the newest of its table, row and own paint.
invariants: a later paint always has a larger stamp
getColor never changes state
chooseWhen: Large tables with few operations
tradeoffs: Lazy stamps use memory per painted row and cell instead of per table cell
hack2hire:69d17a8817b72775cc49bfe0.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: lazy table/row/cell coloring
